name: Autism
summary: Autism is a lifelong and heterogeneous neurodevelopmental condition and, for many people, an identity; clinical descriptions centre on persistent differences in social communication and interaction together with restricted or repetitive patterns that can include sensory features, while abilities and support needs vary widely.

includes: Current clinical descriptions and diagnostic boundaries across the lifespan.
Autistic identity, language preferences and community perspectives.
Sensory experience, co-occurrence, support, access and person-environment fit.
excludes: A single presentation, ability profile or support-needs profile.
Treating one language preference, intervention goal or explanatory model as right for every autistic person.
Treating executive-function or sensory findings as diagnostic of autism by themselves.

claims.text: Autism is a diverse neurodevelopmental condition whose abilities, disabilities and support needs vary substantially between people and can change with age, environment and circumstances.
Sensory hyperreactivity, hyporeactivity and unusual sensory interests can be part of autistic experience, but sensory profiles are heterogeneous and sensory differences are not unique to autism.
Many autistic adults prefer identity-first language such as 'autistic person', but preferences vary within and between cultures and no single terminology should be imposed on every person.
Useful autism support should be based on the person's goals, communication, needs and context rather than assuming that reducing visible autistic traits is automatically the desired outcome.

sources.citation: World Health Organization. Autism fact sheet. 17 September 2025.

uncertainties.question: How can autism evidence and public guidance better represent non-speaking people, people with intellectual disability and people with very high support needs?
uncertainties.why_it_matters: Research samples and online preference studies can systematically underrepresent people whose communication and support needs are greatest.
what_would_reduce_it: Accessible participatory studies using multiple communication methods and deliberate sampling across intellectual ability and support needs.

uncertainties.question: Which sensory measures predict useful, person-defined accommodations across settings?
uncertainties.why_it_matters: Group-level sensory findings do not identify what will help a particular autistic person.
what_would_reduce_it: Ecologically valid, participatory trials of accommodations reporting benefit, burden and adverse effects.

uncertainties.question: How do autism language preferences vary across cultures, languages, ages, communication modes and support needs?
uncertainties.why_it_matters: Current preference studies are disproportionately online and do not represent the full autistic population.
what_would_reduce_it: Accessible multilingual preference research with broader sampling and options beyond a forced identity-first/person-first choice.

uncertainties.question: Which supports improve outcomes that autistic people themselves value, for whom, and under what environmental conditions?
uncertainties.why_it_matters: An intervention can change a measured behaviour without improving autonomy, participation, safety or quality of life.
what_would_reduce_it: Preregistered studies using person-defined outcomes, longer follow-up, adverse-effect reporting and meaningful autistic involvement in study design.

perspectives.held_by: World Health Organization and clinical guidance
perspectives.summary: Autism is a heterogeneous neurodevelopmental condition with widely varying abilities, disabilities and support needs.

perspectives.held_by: Autistic adults represented in language-preference research
perspectives.summary: Identity-first language is often preferred, but substantial variation means individual language preferences should be respected.
Autism research and support should examine social barriers, environment, rights and autistic priorities alongside impairment and clinical needs.
Support should involve autistic adults in decisions and adapt communication, environment and care to individual needs.

relations.note: Autism has been central to neurodiversity discourse; this is not a taxonomic parent-child relation.
Sensory differences are common in autism but heterogeneous and not exclusive to autism.
Executive-function differences are often studied in autism, but they are heterogeneous and not diagnostic of autism.
Autism and ADHD can co-occur; co-occurrence does not make either condition a subtype of the other.

questions: Does the autistic person control and evaluate the accommodation?
Are communication access and safeguarding explicit?
What outcome and context support the claim?
Can the tool increase distress, surveillance or dependency?
Are non-speaking people and people with high support needs represented?
